item.title: I Ran a Marathon. Here’s How It Went.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: Six months of training, one scorching summer in DC and 26.2 miles to find out whether it was enough.
item.content:encoded:
I ran my first marathon on Sunday.

Even typing that feels strange. After six months of training and telling everyone my goal, the idea of running a marathon had started to feel almost ordinary. When you work toward something for that long, the excitement is bound to fade a little, and even if you’ve never run a marathon, I’m sure you know that feeling from something else in your life. So sitting here now, I have to remind myself that finishing a marathon is a remarkable thing, and one worth writing about.

Where it started

I’ve been a runner for most of my life. When I was little, my dad would take my brother and me to the park every Saturday morning, and the three of us would race around the perimeter: 5 kilometers, or 3.1 miles. At the time, I resented those Saturday mornings. Looking back, they were the first time I learned the value of discipline. Once we’d pushed through our chilly morning run, the rest of the weekend was ours.

Despite that love-hate relationship, I kept running competitively for the next ten years, right up until I graduated from high school. By then, the farthest I had ever run was 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), and I had no intention of ever going farther.

In college, running became an easy way to stay in shape, but I never had a real goal in mind. That changed in January 2026, the spring of my senior year. Over winter break, I’d been thinking about resolutions for the new year, and “go to the gym consistently” or “stay in shape” felt too vague to ever actually achieve. If I really wanted to better myself, I needed a lofty goal I could work toward every single day. So I decided to train for a half marathon.

Long story short, I finished it (and accidentally ran several more half marathons in training along the way), and in the process, I fell back in love with running in a way I hadn’t since I was a kid. Two days after the race, I signed up for a full marathon.

The training

I signed up for the Marine Corps Marathon on April 20, which gave me 27 weeks to train. Compared to most marathon plans, that was more than enough time to show up on race day fully prepared. What I didn’t account for was that most of that training would happen during a scorching summer in Washington, DC.

Runna’s custom marathon plan became my bible. For the first month and a half, I followed every workout to a T, speed sessions included, and I watched my VO2 max climb on my phone, along with my confidence. Then, in mid-June, I failed my first workout. As the summer got hotter and my pace got slower, I kept struggling. Run after run, I stopped early from exhaustion. My speed sessions turned into easy runs. Soon enough, five days of running a week became four.

By August, I finally realized the only way out was through. If I wanted to cross that finish line, I had to pick myself back up, endure the heat and run anyway. So I committed to fixing my routine (more on that here). I started saying no to evening plans, going to bed at 8:30pm and fueling properly before and after my runs. My runs didn’t get any easier, but I knew consistency was what would get me to race day. For the next two months, I woke up at 5:30am, put on my running clothes before I could talk myself back into bed, and did the hard work, even when it meant coming home dripping with sweat every morning.

There were still plenty of mornings when I fell short of the distance I was supposed to run, or swapped my run for a cycling class, but I knew I was still building something that would carry me on race day. A few weeks out, I completed two 20-mile long runs. Right after each one, I probably would have told you I’d just gotten lucky and had “no idea” how I finished. Looking back, it was the mental grit I’d built training through the summer heat that kept me going.

One of those 20-milers, three weeks before the race, was the defining moment of my training: the moment I finally believed I could run the full 26.2. I meant to take my usual long-run route, but about three miles in, I took a wrong turn. Instead of doubling back, I just kept going. The scenery was just as nice: trees on the cusp of turning for fall, a paved trail, and plenty of people who looked like they might be running the Marine Corps Marathon in three weeks, too. The route threw a series of never-ending rolling hills at me that I hadn’t seen on any other long run, but the novelty of somewhere new, and the podcasts I’d queued up to distract myself, carried me all the way to the end.

Race day

By race day, I had run roughly 800 miles in 27 weeks. For months, I had known exactly what I’d be wearing, which gel I’d take and when, the music and podcasts I’d listen to, where my family and friends would be standing, and which miles of the course, according to dozens of reviews, were the hardest. My training had its ups and downs, but I knew I was about as prepared as I could be.

Since this was my first marathon, finishing was goal enough, but I had loosely set a time goal, too: on a perfect day, I’d be ecstatic with a 3:35 (about 8:10 per mile) and satisfied with a 3:45 (about 8:35 per mile).

I lined up near the 3:30 pacer, not because I planned to run a 3:30, but because I figured I wouldn’t have to weave around as many people. The gun went off at 7:20, and to my surprise, we started shuffling forward almost immediately. The ten-minute gap I’d expected between the first corral and mine turned out to be two. I nearly forgot to start my watch, and my music still wasn’t set up when I crossed the start line. But I was running with the crowd. The race had started, and it was time to put my training to the test.

On every long run, I had practiced taking the first several miles well below race pace, so I’d always have enough left in the tank for the final two-thirds. I knew I had to do the same on race day if I wanted to make it to the end.

So I started slow, letting it sink in that I was about to run nonstop for more than three hours. In the blink of an eye, I reached the first mile marker, and when I glanced at my watch, I was alarmed to see I was more than a minute per mile faster than I’d planned. After a moment of panic, I made myself slow down. If I could treat the first five or so miles as a proper warm-up, I knew I could fly in the second half.

The energy of the crowd was incredible. I had assumed most of the course would be quiet, since so much of the route is out of the way, but within minutes, thousands of people lined the streets with signs, cheering. My adrenaline was higher than I ever could have imagined, and I had to fight it to save my energy. Every mile marker seemed to arrive within seconds, and despite my best efforts to hold back, I kept speeding up. My head knew I couldn’t sustain that pace, but my body felt amazing. By mile 13, the halfway point, I was effortlessly clicking off 7:40 miles. I looked down at my watch and realized I had just beaten my half marathon PR by four minutes.

Not good.

It was time to take this “slowing down” thing seriously, because if it didn’t happen by choice, it would happen by force within the next few miles.

Sure enough, by mile 17, I was gassed. The crowds were still amazing, but it was clear the last nine miles would be a battle. Luckily, my family and friends were spread out between miles 17 and 19, which gave me just enough of a boost to push through the pain. After mile 19, though, I wouldn’t see a familiar face until the finish.

My dad handed me a water bottle right before the most notoriously difficult part of the course: the 14th Street Bridge, roughly two miles of highway in direct sun. No spectators are allowed, so all you have are your own thoughts and the sight of runners, one after another, slowing to a walk. Several minutes into that excruciating stretch, my watch buzzed: 10% battery remaining. My heart sank. I still had six miles to go, and there was no way my watch would make it to the finish.

Over and over, negative thoughts crept in, telling me the only way I’d make it was to walk. Fighting them felt nearly impossible, until I remembered I had planned for exactly this moment. Once my thoughts started to overwhelm me, I would switch my headphones from music to a podcast to drown out the noise. So I did. All I had to do was listen to the voices in my ears, and I’d be at the finish line in less than an hour. (Oh, and of course I started recording the rest of my run on Strava, because what was the point of any of this if I couldn’t post about it afterward? Kidding.)

The negative thoughts kept coming back every few minutes, but each time, I told myself to just listen to the podcast and run to the next water station. Somehow, I made it to mile 22. Only four to go. As the pain grew and my legs got heavier, the crowds started to come back.

Mile 23. I looked down to check my pace, and right on cue, my watch died. I had less than three miles left: somewhere between 20 and 30 more minutes of running. By then, 3:35 was out the window. All I hoped for was not to DNF.

Mile 24. Only two left. Everyone around me looked like they were in agony, but most of them were still running. If I could keep pushing a little longer, I’d be done. Mile 24 went on forever. At one point, I couldn’t remember whether I’d already passed mile 25 and somehow missed the marker. Then, out of the corner of my eye, I saw it: mile 25. I knew I would make it. There was no world in which I’d walk this close to the finish, so I kept running.

At mile 26, all that stood between me and the end was one short hill. When the sign came, it was time to empty the tank. I picked up the pace as much as my body would let me and braced myself for the climb. With the finish line in sight, I spotted the race clock, which, remember, was running two minutes ahead of my actual time. It read 3:34:20.

It took me a second to register. Unless I collapsed in the next two minutes, I was going to beat my goal, by some miracle. I watched the clock tick toward 3:35 and, with my last ounce of energy, crossed the finish line just as it hit 3:35:02. With my watch dead, I didn’t know my exact time, but I knew it was faster than my loftiest dreams for this race. Holding back tears, I took a water from the nearest Marine, and then a medal was placed around my neck.

What’s next

Just like everyone said it would be, the marathon was the hardest thing I’ve done in my 23 years. It was also the most fulfilling. Choosing to keep running when every voice in my head was telling me to stop is something I’ll remember for the rest of my life. The marathon showed me how strong I really am, and I get to carry that confidence into every hurdle that comes next.

Funnily enough, my fate was sealed before I ever ran Marine Corps: a few months ago, I signed up for the 2027 London Marathon through a charity spot. A risky decision? Perhaps. But this race proved it was the right one. As I start my next training block, my eyes are set on running a Boston qualifying time in London next April. Some might call that a lofty goal. I see it as a new chance to prove what more I’m capable of.

This story first appeared on vitalityritual.org.

item.title: How I’m Starting My Winter Arc
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: How I’m defining my priorities, setting intentions and building a plan to stay consistent through the colder months.
item.content:encoded:
As the days get shorter and the weather gets cooler, it gets harder to keep the habits we built during the warm summer months. This is where the winter arc comes in. A winter arc can take many forms, but at its core, it’s a commitment to staying consistent and accountable to your goals through the colder months. Some people embrace it by starting a fitness challenge like 75 Hard; others take a more holistic approach, simply redefining their priorities and committing to them.

Having finished my first marathon just a few days ago, I see my winter arc taking the holistic route: prioritizing recovery and maintaining my fitness before my London Marathon training block begins in mid-December. Here’s how I’m actually starting mine.

Defining my priorities

This is something I’ve spent the last several months reflecting on. Graduating from college and starting a 9-to-5 makes you hyper-aware of how little time there is outside of work. If you want to be happy, you pretty much have to define your priorities and intentionally set time aside for them. Mine fall into seven buckets:

  • Fitness
  • Career
  • Nutrition
  • Rest and recovery
  • Reading and learning
  • Entrepreneurship
  • Relationships

That might look like a lot of buckets, but ask yourself this: if there were more hours in the day, what would my perfect day look like? The question lets you think aspirationally. To keep it grounded in reality, picture your perfect weekday, and account for however much time you’d usually spend working.

For me, that day looks something like this:

  1. Wake up at 5 a.m.
  2. Hydrate, have a little caffeine, and eat a pre-run snack
  3. Go on a 5-mile run
  4. Stretch, shower, do a full skincare routine with eye masks, and get ready for work
  5. Spend an hour on entrepreneurial work (writing an article for VIRI, website planning, etc.)
  6. Walk to work and call a loved one on the way
  7. Work 9 to 5
  8. Walk home
  9. Make dinner
  10. Read or take a class for about an hour
  11. Go to sleep by 8:30 or 9 p.m.

Setting my intentions

The funny thing is that this schedule isn’t much different from how I already spend my days. There are just a few pieces I need to be more intentional about, and figuring out what those pieces are is how I’ll build my winter arc. The ones I want to spend more focused time on are my entrepreneurial work, my relationships, cooking, and reading and learning.

Now it’s time to set an intention for each priority, with extra attention on the areas I want to improve:

Fitness

Run three days a week, take fitness classes two days a week, and start a weightlifting routine about once a week.

Career

Work proactively: spot potential problems and solve them before they take shape, and build systems that help the firm run better and grow. If I do all of this well, I should earn my bonus and a promotion.

Nutrition

Meal prep every week, balancing carbs, protein, and vegetables. Cook dinner for myself two to three times a week. Avoid processed food and too much caffeine. Drink about 50 ounces of water a day.

Rest and recovery

Get eight hours of sleep every night. Stretch after every workout, no matter how easy it felt.

Reading and learning

Read every day, including the news, and finish at least one book a month. Explore graduate programs and online classes, and make an enrollment plan before January.

Entrepreneurship

Publish two to three articles a week and post on social media weekly.

Relationships

Call loved ones every week and make plans with friends about once a week.

Creating a structured action plan

Defining your goals is fairly easy; putting them into practice is what takes work. You know yourself best, so ask yourself: when have I successfully changed a habit? Really think about it. How did you actually change your behavior? Was it because you made a verbal commitment and didn’t want to break your word? Was it because you wrote the goal down and checking it off kept you motivated? We’re all motivated differently. Over time, I’ve learned that external accountability and systems I can measure are what help me stick to my goals.

Knowing that, it’s time to decide how I’ll actually stay accountable. Here’s the plan, category by category:

Fitness

  • Sign up for workout classes a week in advance.
  • Post my runs on Strava and track my weekly mileage.
  • Tell my boyfriend my weightlifting goal and have him check in on it once a week.

Career

  • Meet with my boss weekly and use his feedback to gauge my performance.

Nutrition

  • Block off two hours every weekend for meal prep.
  • Make a list before grocery shopping each week.
  • Refill my water bottle at work at least twice a day.

Rest and recovery

  • My alarm is always set for 5:15 a.m., so I have to be in bed by 8:30 p.m. (I already have this down pretty well, so I don’t need a super structured plan here.)

Reading and learning

  • Join a book club, a group commitment to reading one book each month.
  • Put one hour on my calendar each week to explore graduate programs and online classes.

Entrepreneurship

  • The weekly newsletter keeps me putting out content consistently.
  • An action-item spreadsheet with deadlines keeps me on top of my to-dos.

Relationships

  • Keep one social event on my calendar each week.
  • End every day with zero unread texts.
  • Set aside one morning a week to call loved ones on my walk to work.

And with that, my winter arc is planned. There will be weeks that don’t go according to plan, and that’s okay! The goal is progress and consistency, not perfection. Happy goal setting!

This story first appeared on vitalityritual.org.
